newsitem.title: USA: Simpson judge asked to throw out framing theory.
newsitem.headline: Simpson judge asked to throw out framing theory.

text.p: Lawyers for the families of murder victims Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman asked a judge on Tuesday to prevent O.J. Simpson from introducing during his civil trial the theory that he was framed.

The former football star's defence team in his criminal trial had implied, but had not produced evidence to support their theory, that vital evidence, such as the bloody glove found at his home after the murders, as well as certain blood samples, had been planted by police.

Simpson was found not guilty of the June 12, 1994, murders of his ex-wife and Goldman by a criminal jury a year ago this week. He was sued in a civil wrongful-death lawsuit by the families of the victims.

In court papers filed on Tuesday lawyers for the Goldman family, led by attorney Daniel Petrocelli, said that legal documents filed recently by Simpson's attorney, Robert Baker, despite being more than 100 pages, were "devoid of evidence" to support the defendant's theories of planted evidence.
Simpson sought to argue in the civil case that Los Angeles police officers planted evidence in a bid to frame him for the murders.
But Petrocelli, in his written argument, urged that Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki's original ruling, that Simpson had to provide evidence of planting before it could be introduced in court, should stand.

"It is time for the court to end this long-running charade. Defendant's 'evidence' is not - and never has been - sufficient to permit him to make the highly charged, inflammatory, confusing, time-consuming and ultimately absurd argument that a network of LAPD police officers, detectives, criminalists and laboratory technicians, most of whom did not know each other, worked together ... to intentionally plant evidence against Simpson to frame him for a capital crime ..." Petrocelli wrote.

Meanwhile, as the process of selecting a jury for the civil trial continued, four people who said they thought Simpson probably committed the murders were added to the pool of jurors retained for further questioning.

So far in the first phase of jury selection in which panellists were asked what they knew of Simpson's criminal trial, 20 of 62 jurors selected to advance to the second phase of questioning said they believed Simpson guilty based on that trial.

Among those who told Judge Fujisaki and lawyers for both sides on Tuesday that they believed Simpson was probably guilty was a black man about 40 who said he believed Simpson's blood was at the crime scene, "but how it got there is certainly debatable."

The man, the first black man questioned in the civil trial to say he thought Simpson was probably guilty, also criticised the Los Angeles police for its investigation of the murders and the handling of crucial blood evidence. "They made mistakes, they weren't perfect," he said.

A white man in his 30s, who said the DNA evidence presented against Simpson in the criminal trial was "compelling," that there was no evidence of any other suspects and that Simpson was "violent and hit his wife on many occasions," was also retained.

A white man in his sixties said he initially felt sympathy for Simpson when he learned of his arrest, but came to think he had probably committed the murders after he fled his home in a famous slow-speed police chase, while a white man in his thirties said he was surprised at the criminal case jury's not guilty verdicts.

The other two prospective jurors retained for further questioning during Tuesday morning's session were a white woman and a black woman, both of whom said they had not followed the criminal trial closely and had no opinions on Simpson's guilt or innocence. Seven black jurors and four white jurors were excused.
